title: The energy break-even
summary: A spiking net does less work only when spikes are rare enough.

terms.definition: Multiply-accumulate. The usual cost of one connection in a non-spiking network, paid whether or not the unit was active.

terms.plain: when spike work equals dense work
terms.definition: The activity level where SynOps cost the same as the MACs they replace. Below it, spikes save work. Above it, they do not.

cards.text:
A regular network multiplies every connection,
even when that unit was silent.

lines: If 2 spikes arrive, the spiking network does about 2 SynOps.

cards.text:
Break-even is the activity where the SynOps cost the same as those MACs.
Rarer than that, spikes win. Busier than that, they do not.

question.prompt: 100 connections, 2 spikes. Who does less work?
question.why: 2 SynOps against 100 MACs. The spikes are well below break-even.
question.simpler: Compare the number of spike crossings with the number of connections.

question.prompt: If every neuron spikes on every step, the spiking network still does less work.
question.why: Then you pay a SynOp on every connection, and the addressing of spikes on top.
question.simpler: Sparsity is the whole saving. A dense rate spends it.

recall.question: When does a spiking network do less work than a dense one?
recall.answer: When spikes are rare enough to sit below the break-even.

deeper.note: This is an operation-count argument, not a measurement on a particular machine. The 2019 Nature perspective is the checklist for when the argument is real.

paper.title: Towards spike-based machine intelligence with neuromorphic computing
paper.section: Read the comparison of encoding, algorithm, and hardware as three separate claims.
